claims.sentence: You will find that the university regulation maps letter grades to a five-point system: A is Excellent, B is Good, C is Satisfactory, D is Fail, P is Passed, and F is Fail
Grades A, B, C, and P are positive and cannot be retaken for improvement, except where the regulation specifies otherwise
Grades D and F are unsatisfactory
Instructors may use alternative grading systems instead of the university standard

If they do, the grading system, evaluation criteria, and conversion rules must be written in the course syllabus or internship program and shared with you through the university's electronic educational environment
If a course page states a grading rule that differs from or goes beyond this regulation, the regulation takes precedence
Out of 275 courses, 103 state a grading scale that pairs letter grades with point ranges, while 172 do not
The typical scale assigns A to 90–100 points, B to 75–89, C to 60–74, and D to 0–59, and 54 of the 103 courses use it
The remaining 49 courses use 21 different scales, and no other scale appears in more than 6 courses

Among the 103 courses that publish a scale, the lowest point threshold for an A is typically 90, shared by 60 courses, while 22 courses use 85, 12 use 80, 2 use 92, and 1 course each uses 136, 95, 96, 104, 84, and 86
The lowest threshold for a B is typically 75, shared by 67 courses, while 13 courses use 70, 6 courses use 80, 6 use 60, 6 use 65, and 1 course each uses 102, 66, 84, 72, and 71
The lowest threshold for a C is typically 60, shared by 70 courses, while 12 courses use 50, 6 use 40, 3 use 65, 3 use 55, 2 use 56, 2 use 70, 2 use 51, and 1 course each uses 68 and 45
The lowest threshold for a D is 0 in 102 courses
Two courses use raw point ranges where the top of grade A exceeds 100

Scales with overlapping or incomplete ranges appear in 4 courses with A 85–100, B 75–84, C 60–75, D 0–59; 1 course with A 136–170, B 102–135, C 68–101, D 0–68; 2 courses with A 92–100, B 80–91, C 65–79, D 0–59; 2 courses with A 85–100, B 80–84, C 51–79, D 0–59; 5 courses with A 85–100, B 75–85, C 60–74, D 0–59; 1 course with only B 75–84; and 1 course with A 85–100, B 70–84, C 50–69, D 0–50
When you look at program levels, 56 BSc courses, 40 MSc courses, and 7 other program courses publish a scale
Of those, 31 BSc courses, 17 MSc courses, and 6 other program courses follow the most common scale
The regulation does not specify how alternative grading systems must be structured, only that they must be documented in syllabuses and communicated electronically
The regulation is silent on whether alternative systems must use letter grades, point ranges, or other formats
The course data does not explain why 172 courses omit a grading scale entirely
The evidence does not clarify how the 2 courses with raw points above 100 calculate totals
The evidence does not state what happens if a course page contradicts the official regulation, only that the regulation outranks course pages
The evidence does not cover how grades P and F are converted to points in alternative systems
The evidence does not explain the exception mentioned in clause 6.1 for retaking positive grades
A regulation that is silent on something does not make a course page wrong
